feed.title: Project Scroll
feed.subtitle: An online treasure hunt through real history, from the St. Joseph River Valley. Every clue is true.

entry.title: Eleven more old postcards

entry.title: A paper passport, a teachers’ pack and a recipe booklet
entry.summary: Printables: a passport booklet with a stamp box for every place, a one-day field trip with two worksheets for teachers, and the valley kitchen as a little book.

entry.title: Who was in town in 1860?
entry.summary: 331 names from the business directories printed beside the old town plans, with the men of Company D, in one roll you can search.

entry.title: Where Kellogg made its telephone cabinets
entry.summary: For years the oak cases of Kellogg telephones and switchboards were made in Cassopolis. An old postcard shows the plant, the lumber stacked by the railroad, and the words “Cabinet Shops” painted on the wall.

entry.title: A depot, a water tower and three clues
entry.summary: An old real-photo postcard of a station somewhere in the valley. Can you name the town?

entry.title: Five minutes with Roosevelt at Dowagiac
entry.summary: On Saturday, 30 March 1912, Theodore Roosevelt’s train stopped at Dowagiac on its way across Michigan. Oscar C. Haight’s camera caught the crowd.

entry.title: The night 3,000 were invited to the Oliver Hotel
entry.summary: James Oliver, the plow maker, built South Bend a grand hotel at Main and Washington. It opened the week before Christmas 1899 and stood until 1967.

entry.title: The Newton House, a farmhouse museum near Decatur
entry.summary: One family lived in this Volinia Township house from 1844 to 1930. Today it is a museum, open on the first Sunday of each month from June to September.

entry.title: The hotel that walked away
entry.summary: In 1867 the old hotel where the lodge held its ball was hauled across Cassopolis and turned into a mill. Where did it end up?

entry.title: The harvest trail: a mill, an orchard and the stove town
entry.summary: Stamp three places in your passport this fall, from September to November, and earn the harvest badge.

entry.title: The day 3,000 people came to watch one log
entry.summary: Twenty-four men carried the first log of the Pioneer Log Cabin while a band played. Four weeks later the cabin was finished.

entry.title: The courthouse that became the Colonial
entry.summary: The Colonial Opera House on a card of 1913 had served Cass County as its courthouse for more than half a century before it was moved across the village.

entry.title: Summer on Diamond Lake: Forest Hall and the island
entry.summary: A tennis net on the lawn, a windmill over the roof and the name along the ridge: Forest Hall, 1909. Across the water, a hotel on an island, with a cannon on its grass.

entry.title: Springbrook Park, halfway between two cities
entry.summary: For more than sixty years the park on the river between South Bend and Mishawaka gave the valley baseball, a summer theatre, band concerts and rides. Very little of it is left.

entry.title: Send someone an old postcard
entry.summary: Pick any card in the gallery, write on the back, and share it from your phone.

entry.title: Race day at the Cassopolis fair grounds
entry.summary: A horse and sulky on the track, a crowd at the rail and a covered grandstand behind. Whose track was it, and where did the county fair run its races?

entry.title: Pick a date, and see what’s open
entry.summary: Tell the Visit & Plan page the day you’re coming. It shows the museums open that day, what’s on, and your own day on the map.

entry.title: City Hall, Mishawaka, and the mayor on the card
entry.summary: A postcard of 1910 names the building and the man in charge of it. Who was Mayor Herzog, and where did his city hall go?

entry.title: Eleven more old postcards
entry.summary: The Pioneer Log Cabin going up in 1923, the depots at Cassopolis and Vandalia, Chicago Street in Edwardsburg, Main Street in Niles and a steam shovel at White Pigeon.

entry.title: Edwardsburg in 1910, through J. Inbody’s camera
entry.summary: A meat market and a bakery, a druggist selling ice cream soda next to the post office, and a frame school with a bell tower. Three cards by an Indiana photographer who made picture postcards.

entry.title: A lodge of E Clampus Vitus, in Cassopolis, in 1846
entry.summary: What two county histories record about the lodge of 1846, and why it matters. Plus five more stories, and a picture for every story.

entry.title: A lodge of E Clampus Vitus, in Cassopolis, in 1846
entry.summary: Two county histories record a lodge of the “Ancient and Honorable Order of Eclampsus Vitus” at Cassopolis, Michigan, in the spring of 1846: four charter members named, a ball of two hundred badges, and the earliest lodge of the order yet found with its members named. Newspapers of the same year show the order already at work across the state line in Indiana. Here is the whole record, what it does and does not prove, and the questions still open.

entry.title: Dr. Goodwin’s hotel on Broadway
entry.summary: A Civil War cavalry captain who became the village doctor built a hotel on Broadway and kept it himself. It took guests into the 1950s, and nothing of it is left.

entry.title: Company D: the 85 men Dowagiac sent in 1861
entry.summary: Raised at Dowagiac in the summer of 1861: who they were, where they fought, and the nineteen who did not come home.

entry.title: Who told Shepard?
entry.summary: The only account of the 1846 lodge was written by a man who was a small child when it happened. Somebody told him. Who?

entry.title: Band night at French’s Hotel, Eagle Lake
entry.summary: A brass band on folding chairs under the trees, a flag strung overhead, and buggies and motor cars drawn up behind. A summer evening at Eagle Lake, on a card of 1912.
